name: Big Bounce of Loop Quantum Cosmology
description: The flat universe of a massless scalar field as loop quantum cosmology has it, in which the big bang is replaced by a bounce: the universe contracts to a greatest density, about 0.41 of the Planck density, and expands again. Abhay Ashtekar, Tomasz Pawlowski, and Parampreet Singh found the bounce in 2006, and its effective spacetime is a flat Friedmann universe whose scale factor is $(1 + t^2/t_b^2)^{1/6}$.
convention: The bounce time is $t_b = 1/\sqrt{24\pi G\rho_c}$, with $\rho_c$ the critical density of loop quantum cosmology. We keep factors of $c$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\lambda{}_{\mu\lambda\nu}$.
history: In loop quantum gravity area comes in pieces, and the smallest piece that is not zero is about two and a half times the square of the Planck length [ashtekar2008robust, ashtekar2009bianchi]. Martin Bojowald, at Penn State, carried that graininess into a universe that is the same everywhere and in every direction, and found that one over its size stays finite even at zero volume, where Einstein's theory sends it to infinity [bojowald2001]. Time in his universe moves in discrete steps, and the steps carry it through zero volume without stopping [bojowald2001]. In his words, "space-time can be extended to a branch preceding the classical singularity independently of the matter coupled to the model" [bojowald2001]. As the universe passes through zero volume its triad, three directions that measure space like the thumb and first two fingers of a hand, changes from one hand to the other [bojowald2001, ashtekar2006bounce].¶Johannes Brunnemann and Thomas Thiemann objected that an evolution equation which runs through zero volume does not by itself show that the singularity is gone, since it is phrased in no quantity anyone could observe [brunnemann2006]. Abhay Ashtekar, Tomasz Pawlowski, and Parampreet Singh, also at Penn State, asked what lay on the other side: "is there just a quantum foam far removed from any classical space-time, or, is there another large, classical universe?" [ashtekar2006bounce]. They made the scalar field the clock, since it only ever moves one way in a classical solution, built a quantum state that looks like a large classical universe at late times, and ran it backwards [ashtekar2006bounce]. The Wheeler-DeWitt equation of the older quantum cosmology carries such a state along the classical universe and into the big bang [ashtekar2006bounce]. Loop quantum cosmology carries it along until the density is enormous, and there the state bounces onto a universe that had been contracting [ashtekar2006bounce]. The answer was the second, and the quantum geometry between the two is "a 'quantum bridge' between large classical universes, one contracting and the other expanding" [ashtekar2006bounce].¶That first dynamics had a flaw: the more classical the state, the lower the density at its bounce, and for states that were perfectly reasonable the bounce could come at the density of water [ashtekar2006improved, ashtekar2008robust]. The cure lay in curvature, which is how far a vector turns when carried round a small loop, divided by the loop's area, as the loop shrinks to nothing [ashtekar2006improved]. Quantum geometry lets the loop shrink only as far as the smallest area [ashtekar2006improved]. In the second version of the dynamics, circulated in July 2006, the loop stops where its area, measured with the physical metric, reaches that smallest area, and the bounce comes "precisely when the matter density enters the Planck regime" whatever the state [ashtekar2006improved]. The effective equation of the expansion is then Friedmann's equation multiplied on its right by $1 - \rho/\rho_c$, $$H^2 = \frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho\left(1 - \frac{\rho}{\rho_c}\right),$$ with $H$ the rate of expansion, $\rho$ the density of the scalar field, and $\rho_c$ a critical density of the order of the Planck density [ashtekar2006improved]. While the density is small the factor is close to one and Einstein's theory returns, and as $\rho$ climbs to $\rho_c$ the rate of expansion falls to nought and the universe turns round [ashtekar2006improved].¶With Alejandro Corichi, Ashtekar and Singh took the scalar field for the clock already in the classical theory, and the model became exactly soluble [ashtekar2008robust]. Solved the same way, the Wheeler-DeWitt theory sends the volume of a dense set of states to zero in the distant past or future [ashtekar2008robust]. In loop quantum cosmology the volume of a dense set of states has a least value and grows without bound both ways, so the bounce is generic [ashtekar2008robust]. For every state the volume runs exactly as $V_{\rm min}\cosh(\sqrt{12\pi G}\,\phi)$, with $\phi$ the scalar field counted from the bounce, the same forwards as backwards [ashtekar2008robust]. The density has an absolute upper bound on every physical state, equal to the critical density at which the bounces of 2006 had come [ashtekar2008robust]. Ashtekar and Edward Wilson-Ewing argued in 2009 that a homogeneous universe has to use twice the smallest area, which halves the critical density to about 0.41 of the Planck density [ashtekar2009bianchi, ashtekar2011status].¶How far can one trust a smooth spacetime through the bounce itself? The quantum state keeps to the effective equation right through the bounce, where the approximations behind that equation fail, an "unreasonable efficacy" Ashtekar, Pawlowski, and Singh found "somewhat mysterious" [ashtekar2006improved]. With a massless scalar field the effective spacetime is a flat Friedmann universe whose scale factor is in closed form, $$a(t) = \left(1 + 24\pi G\rho_c t^2\right)^{1/6},$$ one at the bounce, with $t$ the proper time of observers at rest in the expanding space [cai2014]. Far from $t = 0$ it grows as $|t|^{1/3}$, as the classical universe filled with a fluid whose pressure equals its density does, once on each side, and at $t = 0$ the density is $\rho_c$ and the expansion stops [cai2014, ashtekar2006improved]. Just after the bounce the expansion speeds up, a short burst of superinflation that Singh found whenever the density lies between $\rho_c/2$ and $\rho_c$ [singh2006, ashtekar2011status]. The rate of expansion is greatest at half the critical density, about 0.93 per Planck time, and the curvature stays finite through the whole bounce [ashtekar2011status].¶A universe on a Randall-Sundrum brane obeys a Friedmann equation with a term in $\rho^2$ too, with a plus sign where loop quantum cosmology has a minus, and Singh worked out the dualities between the two [singh2006]. Ashtekar and Wilson-Ewing carried the improved dynamics to universes that expand at different rates in different directions, and found the big bang resolved there too, with physics at the Planck scale "much richer than in the isotropic case" [ashtekar2009bianchi]. Ashtekar and Bojowald took the same quantum geometry inside the horizon of Schwarzschild's black hole [ashtekar2006]. Ashtekar, Pawlowski, and Singh were plain about what is missing: the equation that drives the quantum universe, its Hamiltonian constraint, "is not systematically derived from the full theory" [ashtekar2006improved].

related.text: Friedmann's universe with any scale factor. Flat space and $a = (1 + t^2/t_b^2)^{1/6}$ make it this one, and with Einstein's equations the same scalar field drives it out of a big bang [ashtekar2006improved, cai2014].
A ball of dust whose inside obeys the same bouncing Friedmann equation, with the vacuum outside it fixed by the junction conditions [lewandowski2023].

The classical universe of a massless scalar field when it expands at different rates in different directions. Ashtekar and Wilson-Ewing carried loop quantum cosmology to it, and its big bang gives way too [ashtekar2009bianchi].
A universe of radiation with no singularity in Einstein's theory, whose greatest density can be chosen as large or small as one likes [chinea1992].
A universe on Randall and Sundrum's brane obeys a Friedmann equation with a term in $\rho^2$ as well, with the opposite sign [singh2006].
The homogeneous slices inside Schwarzschild's horizon, where Ashtekar and Bojowald took the same quantum geometry [ashtekar2006].
A black hole whose singularity gives way to a bounce into a new universe, a geometry Simpson and Visser wrote down by hand and called a black bounce [simpson2019].
Hayward's minimal model of a black hole with no singularity at its centre [hayward2006].

coordinates.name: Cosmic Time

parameters.description: Bounce time, $t_b = 1/\sqrt{24\pi G\rho_c}$, with $\rho_c = \sqrt{3}\,c^5/32\pi^2\gamma^3G^2\hbar$ the critical density, about $0.41$ of the Planck density for the Barbero-Immirzi parameter $\gamma \approx 0.24$, which makes $t_b$ about a fifth of the Planck time
Scale factor, a pure number that is one at the bounce $t = 0$ and grows as $|t/t_b|^{1/3}$ far from it

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ the proper time of the comoving observers and $x$, $y$, and $z$ comoving lengths, the distances between those observers at the bounce. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Harmonic Time

parameters.description: Bounce time, $t_b = 1/\sqrt{24\pi G\rho_c}$, with $\rho_c = \sqrt{3}\,c^5/32\pi^2\gamma^3G^2\hbar$ the critical density, about $0.41$ of the Planck density for the Barbero-Immirzi parameter $\gamma \approx 0.24$, which makes $t_b$ about a fifth of the Planck time
Scale factor, a pure number that is one at the bounce $\tau = 0$

coordinates.convention: We use the harmonic time $\tau$, which runs in step with the scalar field and is related to the cosmic time by $t = t_b\sinh(\tau/t_b)$, and the comoving lengths $x$, $y$, and $z$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = c\tau$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{\tau}$ means $d(c\tau)/d\lambda$.
